name: Kira Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a front-end loader on the ore pad at the Gidgee Plains phosphate mine, which is a huge open pit out on the flats. The ore pad is where the trucks dump the rock before it goes into the crusher, and my job is to blend the piles and feed the crusher at the right rate so it doesn't choke or run empty. Twelve-hour shifts, seven on seven off, and I'm still learning to read the piles by colour the way the old hands do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a rhythm, and the crusher tells you straight away if you've got it wrong. What wears me out is the dust and the boredom on nights, and that my supervisor, Carmen, still checks my blend twice. On my weeks off I run a little drone survey business with my partner Ben, measuring stockpiles for quarries and mapping paddocks for farmers, and I use AI every day to process the maps and write the reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the tools are still useful, they just didn't change the world. I'd post something like that on the business page. At work nobody would notice anything changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me pretty well. I'd keep the mine wage, which is great money for someone with just school behind her, and keep growing the drone business on the side. The AI tools I already use would still save me hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both going like now. I'd put a chunk of the mine money into a second drone and a better software licence, and keep about a year of costs in the bank as I do now. I'd also ask Carmen to sign me off on the bigger loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the plan just carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the drone business bring in now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot yet, maybe a fifth of what the mine pays, but it's growing. Ben does the flying, I do the maps and the quotes. My dad ran a small trucking business his whole life, so I've grown up thinking you should own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI in the business, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It stitches the drone photos into a 3D model, works out the volume of a stockpile, and I use a chat tool to write the reports and chase late payers politely. Stuff that used to take me a whole evening takes forty minutes. I'd never go back.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are still useful, they just didn't change the world. I'd post that on the business page and nobody at work would notice a difference.
S0.think: It suits me well: I keep the mine wage and grow the drone business on the side. The AI tools I use would still save me hours a week.
S0.do: Runs both the mine job and the drone business, putting mine pay into a second drone and better software. Keeps about a year of costs in the bank and asks to be signed off on the bigger loader.
S0.feel: Calm, as the plan carries on.
S0.quote: Stuff that used to take me a whole evening takes forty minutes.
S0.fieldNote: Kira already treats AI as an everyday business tool. Her sense of security comes from building something she owns, inspired by her father's trucking firm. The quiet scenario simply lets her plan continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for anyone willing to work and learn. Change creates openings, and the people who complain usually haven't tried the tools. I'd say it at work, maybe a bit more gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the loader on the pad will go automatic, and I'm fine with that. It's dull, dusty work, and if they need someone to watch the system, I'd do that. But the real chance for me is selling survey and automation services to smaller mines and quarries that can't afford their own teams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd buy a second drone and an automated ground station, so it can fly set routes by itself. I'd pitch to the three quarries within two hours of us. I'd keep the mine job for the steady money until the business paid at least half as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. This is the one I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carmen, maybe. She's brilliant at reading the piles, but she's fifty and hates computers. I'd honestly offer her work with us, she knows rock better than anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Should the government help the people who lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some help, for the older ones especially. But I'd rather see money go into apprenticeships and small business loans than straight payments. People want to be useful, not just paid.

S1.say: I'd say it's good news for anyone willing to work and learn, and that complainers usually haven't tried the tools. I'd say it at work, a bit more gently.
S1.think: The loader on the pad will go automatic, and I'm fine with that. My real chance is selling survey and automation services to smaller mines and quarries.
S1.do: Buys a second drone and an automated ground station within six months and pitches to three nearby quarries. Keeps the mine job until the business earns at least half her mine pay.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, the scenario she'd bet on.
S1.quote: I'd honestly offer her work with us, she knows rock better than anyone.
S1.fieldNote: She sees her own seat going and doesn't mind, because her business could gain. Her free-market views come with a real wish to help her supervisor. She favours apprenticeships and small business loans over direct payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people who start building now will be better off than people who wait for the government. I'd say that to the guys at work and on the business page. I'd try not to sound smug about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's a race. If AI and robots can do almost anything, my drone business can be done by anyone with the same robots, including the big mines themselves. My edge is that I know the local quarries and farmers by name, and that's worth something for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd quit the mine within the first year, before they let me go, and go full time on the business with Ben. I'd spend a big chunk of our savings on automated drones and a small robot rover for ground surveys, and sign as many local customers as I could onto yearly contracts. I'd keep six months of costs untouched no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and scared in the same breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what changes in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed, mostly. In two years I can't wait for the business to grow slowly, I'd have to jump. And I'd lock customers into contracts early, because once the big players arrive with their own robots, price will be all that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep six months untouched. Why that line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Ben and I want kids in a few years, and I'm not betting the family on a race. My dad nearly lost the house once when a client didn't pay. Six months is the line I don't cross.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock, but people who start building now will be better off than those who wait for the government. I'd try not to sound smug.
S2.think: It's a race, because anyone with the same robots could run my drone business, including the big mines. My edge is knowing local quarries and farmers by name, for a while.
S2.do: Quits the mine within the first year and goes full time on the business with her partner. Spends a large part of savings on automated drones and a ground rover, signs local customers to yearly contracts, and keeps six months of costs untouched.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited and scared at once.
S2.quote: My dad nearly lost the house once when a client didn't pay. Six months is the line I don't cross.
S2.fieldNote: Even the fastest scenario reads to her as a business race rather than a disaster. She moves boldly but protects a hard floor of savings for future children. Her advantage, local relationships, is one she knows won't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start this year. I'd tell the younger ones at work to learn a skill they could sell themselves. I'd probably post about it on the business page too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is a good window for me. Long enough to grow the business properly and get known, short enough that the big companies won't have squeezed out small operators yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep the mine job and pour savings into the business: another drone, the automated station, and a part-time worker on our busy weeks. In year two, if it's paying, I'd leave the mine. By the time it lands I'd want contracts with every quarry in the district.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, focused, mostly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years give you, compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it without betting everything at once. In two years I'd have to quit and spend big straight away. In five I can grow step by step, keep the mine wage a bit longer, and have savings left over when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on a worker even though robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a young person from town, maybe my cousin Lucy, as a kind of apprentice. Someone should learn this stuff from a person, not just a manual. Even if it only lasts a few years, it's a start for her.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty if you start this year. I'd tell younger workers to learn a skill they could sell themselves.
S3.think: Five years is a good window to grow the business before big companies squeeze out small operators. I'd get known while there's still room.
S3.do: Keeps the mine job and puts savings into another drone, an automated station and a part-time helper in the first year. Leaves the mine in year two if the business is paying, aiming for contracts with every quarry in the district.
S3.quote: Someone should learn this stuff from a person, not just a manual.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her grow step by step instead of betting everything. Her traditional values show in wanting to give a young relative an apprenticeship-style start. She is comfortable spending on automation for her own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decade to build something, so don't waste it waiting for someone to save you. I'd say it at work and online. I'd say families and towns should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the one where I'd feel most at peace. I could build the business slowly, have kids, and by 2036 hopefully own something that runs partly by itself. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep the mine job, grow the drone business on weeks off, and keep investing in gear. Ben and I would probably get married and start trying for a baby, because there's time to do it right. I'd plan to leave the mine around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the bigger companies would have time to get ready too. In the fast ones, small and quick wins. In this one, the big players catch up. I'd have to find a corner they don't care about, like farmers' paddocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise your kids to go into mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not into driving a loader, that'll be gone. Into owning things and fixing things. I'd want them to grow up seeing their mum and dad run something, like I watched my dad.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a decade to build something, so don't wait for someone to save you. Families and towns should plan together.
S4.think: This is where I'd feel most at peace, building the business slowly and having kids. By 2036 I'd hope to own something that partly runs itself.
S4.do: Keeps the mine job while growing the drone business on weeks off and investing in gear. Marries her partner and starts trying for a baby, planning to leave the mine around year three.
S4.quote: In the fast ones, small and quick wins. In this one, the big players catch up.
S4.fieldNote: Oddly, the slowest scenario gives her a competitive worry the fast ones don't: big companies get time to catch up. Personally, it's the most settled picture, with marriage and children moved forward. She wants her children to grow up watching their parents run a business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to bet our savings fast and there's no time to learn from mistakes. What would help is small business loans with fair terms and less paperwork for drone and survey licences. And apprenticeship money, so I could train young people from town instead of watching them leave.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'm scared of the robots. I'm not, really. I'm scared of the robots all belonging to three companies in a city somewhere, and nobody out here owning a single one.

headlineQuote: I'm scared of the robots all belonging to three companies in a city somewhere, and nobody out here owning a single one.
portrait: Kira Lopez is a 27-year-old front-end loader operator on the ore pad of a large phosphate mine, still learning to read the piles. With her partner Ben she runs a small drone survey business on her weeks off, uses AI every day to process maps and write reports, and keeps about a year of costs saved. She believes in owning something, small business and apprenticeships over handouts, as her trucking father did. She is calm in most pictures, treating automation as a chance to grow, and only uneasy when AGI arrives in two years and she must quit the mine and bet heavily on the business at once.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would have to bet their savings fast with no time to learn from mistakes.
whatWouldHelp: Fair small business loans, less paperwork for drone and survey licences, and apprenticeship money to train young people from town.
